posts.text: Hopefully it’s a great day spent with your friends and family. And if it’s not, make it a great day anyway!

comments.text: I do the following Thanksgiving assignment each year, and find it really fulfilling. Passing this on from my wonderful college professor Danny Warshay. Copy-pasted-with-some-bits-added: Think of your supporters: Think of all of the people who have helped you get to where you are today. All of the coaches, advisers, supporters, teachers, employers, mentors, relatives and friends. All the people who helped you in the early days of your career, or in your life, or recently. All of the references who spoke on your behalf for jobs. Even the categories, let alone all of the individual supporters, are endless for all of us. That person you meant to thank a decade ago for something they probably forgot by now. Your Assignment: Select one or two, and write them a handwritten note to let them know how you are doing and to thank them for helping you get here. We are all on both sides of this equation from time to time, and we all know how much we enjoy hearing from those whose lives we have influenced, especially hearing those simple and magical words, “Thank you.” To me, it feels like more than ever, we need to find moments of gratitude. I hope your doing this adds a little extra meaning to your Thanksgiving and to the Thanksgiving of those who will be hearing from you! Based on the moving experiences many of you have shared with me that resulted from this simple gesture, I am confident that you will find this rewarding. For those of you who will be celebrating American Thanksgiving, I hope you enjoy what I know is a much-needed break. And for those of you who are not, I hope you will join me in a few moments of gratitude.

posts.title: Tell HN: Lots of Ask HNs again
posts.text: There have been questions about why the /ask page ( https://news.ycombinator.com/ask ) was running dry of Ask HNs - e.g.: Ask HN: Why is Ask HN only showing me 14 posts? - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49984484 - Oct 2026 (47 comments) Ask HN: Why is pagination gone on "Ask HN", and showing only 19 items? - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50280719 - Oct 2026 (3 comments) I believe I found the problem. The pool of stories for https://news.ycombinator.com/ask has traditionally been drawn from the ranked stories list from which we generate the frontpage. That list is restricted to the top 1500 ranked submissions, and it seems the % of submissions which are text posts (i.e. no linked URL) had declined enough to starve the Ask HN feed. The solution is to compute a separate list of ranked Ask HNs. p.s. "Ask HN" is the conventional name but it means text posts. The title can also start with "Tell HN" or nothing in particular. They're just posts which were submitted without a URL.

comments.text: That’s pretty funny! I’ve seen optimizations like this for reporting systems where rather than taking the top N item matching filter X, they cheat by taking the top M (where M > N) items and then filter it client side to N items matching filter X. As long as the results are enough to populate the page you don’t notice the difference and it’s usually faster as you reuse the prior ranking. But if not, you get this exact situation.

posts.title: Ask HN: Anthropic is accusing my company of distilling. How can I prove I'm not?
posts.text: Basically the title. Anthropic is accusing me and my company of using their API for distillation. We are not. We do not train our own models. Our only usage which I think could get us flagged is automated regression benchmarks whenever we change some AI settings. But this is not against their policy? Now I've got 24h to prove we didn't. Has anyone dealt with this too? How can you prove that you are not distilling Anthropic models without breaking your user's privacy?

comments.text: Whatever you submit in 24h, submit the same evidence to Claude and ask it to tell you if it's sufficient evidence to make distilling seem unlikely. Because you know Anthropic is just going to be using Claude as well. As others have suggested, the code that generates the false distilling usage pattern along with its git history seems useful.
comments.author: varenc

comments.text: This happened to me with oai, and I only found out bc of a truly bizarre billing issue and reaching out to friends who were at the company. It took a lot of digging but it turned out they suspected me of distillation and just... didn't tell me. Not saying it's what you should do, but here's what I would do. Basically show you're a good actor and you want to work with them. 1) rotate your keys, and tell them. if your keys were compromised (and lots of keys are) somebody out there COULD be distilling and you would be an "accessory" to it. letting them know that you're rotating JIC is good-actor behavior. 2) don't try to prove something you can't prove. as many have pointed out, there's no way to demonstrate that you aren't distilling. 3) ask for your day in court. tell them you want to use their models and want to clear this up, and ask them to provide you with whatever evidence they have (even if all they can give you is a date range or whatever!) so that you can analyze & respond. if they won't play ball, sucks but tbh it's a big LLM world out there and you have lots of options!

"There will always be causes for anxiety, whether due to prosperity or to wretchedness," like Seneca said. Instead accept that sometimes you will feel anxious, but try to focus on sparking other, more positive feelings that you're looking for. If the anxiety is a problem, look for help learning to cope with it (I like Dr. K's Healthy Gamer videos), but if you're an anxious person like me, don't trick yourself into thinking it'll suddenly disappear some day. 2. In regard to sparking those positive feelings, don't try to make it happen intellectually. Do things. Try stuff out. Treat it as an exploration. Your brain will have one reaction to thinking about something and another to actually doing it. You want to test things and then pay attention and see if they actually spark positive feelings for you. One thing I was sure I would enjoy was volunteer work. I did a bunch of nonprofit volunteering during my free weekends for a few months. Turns out I wasn't a great fit for the ones I tried and didn't super enjoy it. I still admire those organizations and care about what they do, but I feel better giving them monetary support and using my free time doing other things. If I had never actually gone and volunteered, I would have sat around thinking "oh if only I dedicate myself to some great purpose will I be happy." Doing things helped me actually learn about myself. 3. This is sort of an extension of #1, but don't aim for some blissful, uncomplicated future. Almost certainly your whole life—past, present, and future—was, is, and will be some mix of good and bad. We're awash in an achievement, media, and advertising culture that promises us one day all of our problems will be solved. None of that is to say you can't take action in your life and change things, and the end result of those changes may improve the balance, but we all still get old, we all die, tragedies will happen. That's just part of the human condition. But so is fun, joy, curiosity, friendship. So make the most of the good, accept the bad, change what you can, and let go of the idea of total control. Having a fundamental knowledge of how a computer works down to the electrical level makes it a lot easier to pick up new technologies, to guide their development, and generally keep up to speed. As people get further from the bare metal, this knowledge about how computers work seems to be scarcer than it used to be. I think this all means that CS knowledge will remain useful even in the AI era, because knowing how to think and what questions to ask are what you are really learning in a degree program and those will remain rare skills no matter how good AI gets. comments.text: The comments so far appear to be tackling external recruiters however I think you're actually asking about internal recruiters so I'll focus on that. Context: My career started in software engineering before moving into recruitment. I spent a few years agency-side (external) but the majority of my career has been internal (including with a few YC companies). I have about ~15yrs of experience ranging from tech recruiter to Global VP of Talent. Assessing recruiter skills (just like assessing an engineer's skills) varies from company to company. One of the most common metrics is 'time to hire' which is essentially a measure of how long it takes to go from a vacancy going live, to having someone in the seat. Ultimately that is the most useful measure because an ineffective recruiter will take much longer to fill an open role. For me, the next most important measure was essentially a hiring manager NPS. I appreciate you might assume that the candidate NPS is more important however I've found that people you've just given a job to tend to only provide positive feedback on the experience so it's a bit redundant. Another critical measure of efficacy for me is the interview success rate ratio. We'd look at every stage of our hiring pipeline and measure the pass/fail ratio with the goal being as close to a 50/50 split as possible. Having a balance is important because if everyone you interview is good enough to get through to the next stage then either your process is lacking rigour or your standards aren't high enough! This measure also tends to counter the whole "throw shit at the wall and see what sticks" approach. When you're an internal recruiter, one of the biggest values you add to a business is reducing the time the business spends on recruitment so less time interviewing poor quality candidates is critical. On the point of retention rates; I generally don't hold my recruiters accountable for that. Naturally we pay attention to any obvious negative trends but broadly speaking, it's the recruiters job to identify and attract good people, it's the hiring team and hiring managers responsibility to assess them and on-board them properly. It's my job to help the hiring team and hiring managers get better at retention. Happy to answer any other questions you have!

Yes GUI can expose a lot of actions, especially chainable ones like listing results and acting on one of the items. But if I know the exact thing I need, a shell script would be faster. The only thing faster is a set of keyboard shotcuts (think vim, magit, w3m,...). When I'm working on a project for some time ($JOB), I usually end up writing little utilities and makefiles to speed up common tasks. Especially if they are some things I need to do on a regular basis. Sometimes it doesn't pay out in the end. But the whole flow is smoother and thus more delightful. As far as TUI programs go, my interest is mostly in remote machine use and the ubiquity of shortcuts. Old GUI used to have a lot of shortcuts (Just checked and QT in KDE stil supports Alt based navigation (I forgot the exact name)), but now it's just icons and non visible keybindings. Also most TUI can easily shell out to other utilities making integration easy. To recap: I code better when I have smoother workflow, which means easy access to the information I need now (next error from the last run, docs for the current function,...). IDE help but they're usually overfitted to one project style and languages. I ship quicker when I can automate the whole workflow to a series of actions and succinct results I can quickly review. And that means integrating a whole bunch of utilities to a common hub, which is usually a terminal multiplexer (Emacs also works fine for that).
